title: «Σ’ αγαπώ πολύ μαμά μου» – Κινέζα νύφη έμαθε ελληνικά για να κάνει έκπληξη στην πεθερά της
content:
Μια πολύ όμορφη και συγκινητική έκπληξη ετοίμασε για την Ελληνίδα πεθερά της η Shu Lin. Η γυναίκα από την Κίνα αποφάσισε να μάθει ελληνικά κρυφά, ώστε να μπορέσει να της μιλήσει στη γλώσσα της κατά τη διάρκεια της γαμήλιας δεξίωσης στην Ελλάδα.
Η Shu Lin μοιράστηκε στα social media ένα βίντεο από τη συγκινητική στιγμή και εξήγησε την ιστορία πίσω από την προσπάθειά της. Όπως αποκάλυψε, ξεκίνησε να μαθαίνει ελληνικά από τον Απρίλιο. Η πεθερά της γνώριζε ότι έκανε μαθήματα ελληνικών, όμως δεν ήξερε τον πραγματικό λόγο για τον οποίο τα μάθαινε.
Η Shu Lin έλεγε στους φίλους και στους συγγενείς της ότι ήθελε να μάθει ελληνικά κυρίως για να μπορεί να παραγγέλνει φαγητό στα εστιατόρια. Η δικαιολογία αυτή είχε και μια δόση αλήθειας, αφού η αγάπη της για το φαγητό τη βοήθησε να μάθει περισσότερες ελληνικές λέξεις. Ωστόσο, ο πραγματικός της στόχος ήταν διαφορετικός: ήθελε να κρατήσει την εκμάθηση της γλώσσας μυστική, ώστε κανείς από τους Έλληνες φίλους και συγγενείς της να μην αποκαλύψει την έκπληξη.
Η μεγάλη στιγμή ήρθε στη γαμήλια δεξίωση, η οποία πραγματοποιήθηκε στην Ελλάδα, στην οικογενειακή ταβέρνα. Εκεί η Shu Lin κατάφερε να μιλήσει στην πεθερά της στα ελληνικά και να της πει όλα όσα είχε ετοιμάσει εδώ και μήνες.
Η ίδια περιγράφει την πεθερά της ως έναν άνθρωπο γεμάτο αγάπη, δύναμη, ζεστασιά, φροντίδα, γενναιοδωρία και χιούμορ. Από την πρώτη στιγμή, όπως αναφέρει, την υποδέχθηκε με πολλή αγάπη στην οικογένεια και την έκανε να νιώσει ευπρόσδεκτη.
Μέχρι να μάθει καλύτερα ελληνικά, οι δύο γυναίκες επικοινωνούσαν συχνά χρησιμοποιώντας το Google Translate. Η Shu Lin, όμως, συνέχισε να προσπαθεί και κατάφερε τελικά να μιλήσει στην πεθερά της στη μητρική της γλώσσα.
Με το μήνυμά της εξέφρασε την αγάπη, τον σεβασμό και την ευγνωμοσύνη της για τη γυναίκα που την υποδέχθηκε στην οικογένειά της. Ανάμεσα στα λόγια που της είπε ήταν και η φράση που συγκίνησε ιδιαίτερα: «Σ’ αγαπώ πολύ, μαμά μου».

title: I didn't post on social media about my home purchase, marriage, or pregnancy. It made the moments more meaningful.
content:
Years ago, I got a call from a friend. "The most amazing thing happened," she gushed, "we got engaged!" She proceeded to tell me about how her boyfriend proposed. They're such a loving and compatible couple, I couldn't have been happier for them. Days later, I saw the picture online, her finger encrusted with an antique diamond ring, an heirloom from her fiancé's grandmother, just like she had told me about over the phone.
Over the years, I would get a message, sometimes out of the blue, from a friend saying something along the lines of, "Let's catch up." Then we'd set up a time to meet, or, if we lived too far apart, have a phone call. At times, the news was joyful, like a pregnancy or a major step in a relationship. Other times, it was somber, a divorce, a job loss, a tragic health condition.
Sometimes I would see my friends post on social media later, after they had already told me. Each time, I felt honored that they had reached out to me directly. I felt special that they wanted to make sure I knew what was going on in their life, and not just that I was within the blast radius of a social media post.
When it was my turn, I prioritized personal connections
The year 2023 was big for me. At the beginning of the year, my boyfriend and I bought a weekend house in the mountains. That spring, he proposed to me at that weekend house, under a starry sky. We were both in our mid-30s and eager to start a family. That summer, we eloped with an intimate ceremony at the same place we had our first date three years earlier. In the fall, we shared the good news with family and friends that we were expecting our first child.
I felt the temptation to share all my good fortunes with pictures broadcasted across the World Wide Web. But instead of a picture, I sent my friends a message. "Let's get together," or "let's have a call," it said.
Instead of posting the quintessential picture of us holding up a set of keys in front of a house, we told our friends about buying a vacation house over drinks. "We can't wait to see it!" they exclaimed, and we clinked our glasses together in celebration.
When I met up with a friend I hadn't seen in a while, she grabbed my hand mid-hug when the sparkle of the diamond caught her eye. Another friend brought over a housewarming gift. She caught a glimpse of the grainy sonogram picture on the fridge. "I'm so happy for you guys," she said, holding back tears of joy.
Hugs beat out "likes" or heart emojis any day
So much happened in such a short period of time that year. When we caught up with friends we hadn't seen in a couple of months, the answer to "so, what's new with you?" sometimes ended up being "we bought a house, and we got engaged, and now we're married, and we're having a baby!"
Each time I shared the special things going on in my life, I got to experience the joy again, through the other person. Those moments created memories that I would never have had from just posting online. Waiting to share news in person with the people I love, and seeing their reaction, released more endorphins than any number of "likes" to a post.
Technology has helped me stay in touch with my family and friends around the country and the world. I've come to find that sharing life's ups and downs with the people I love, in person when possible, or by call if not, is the best way to stay connected.

One of the world's most valuable rice varieties, basmati carries strong historic ties to the Punjab region, which spans both India and Pakistan.
Both claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.
But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the fight over basmati rice is far from over.

ABVP sweeps DUSU polls as student safety, identity dominate campaign
The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), affiliated with the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), won three of four central posts in this year's Delhi University Students' Union elections, with its candidate Yash Dabas coming in from behind to be elected president.
Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen made history by winning the vice-presidential seat, defeating candidates fielded by both ABVP and the National Students' Union of India (NSUI), the student wing of the Indian National Congress.
In a university facing an acute shortage of hostels, student housing and safety dominated this year's campaign. This came after the September 6 collapse of a paying-guest building in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, which killed seven students.
High rents, non-functional hostels, and a lack of affordable lodging near campus were central issues in candidate platforms.
Declaring his win, Dabas stressed the issue as he addressed the media: "We all witnessed the accident that occurred in Satya Niketan; we do not want such an incident to happen to anyone in the future, and that will be our first priority — conducting safety audits for every college, hostel, and PG."
Shokeen, an NSUI rebel who ran independently, built his campaign partly around the tragedy, vowing not to wear footwear until affected students got justice.
The election also unfolded in the shadow of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led satirical protest movement that organized weeks of demonstrations at Delhi's Jantar Mantar earlier this year, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in national entrance exams.
While the CJP was not involved in the DUSU race directly, the movement shaped how many voters approached the election.
"Students were talking about what or ganisations stand for, whether they agree with their politics and whether voting can give them a greater say in issues concerning students," one student told news agency PTI, adding that many felt they "should not simply vote because a particular organisation has always been influential on campus."
More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee
US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients.
The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status.
Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions.
The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful.
The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%.
When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning.
Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia.
He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit."
Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide
Surendra Koli, a key figure in India's notorious 2006 Nithari serial killings case who was acquitted of all charges last year, was found dead at a tea stall he operated in Haridwar.
Police are treating the case as a suspected suicide.
Residents discovered Koli's body inside the rented stall and alerted authorities, Haridwar City Deputy Superintendent of Police Shishupal Singh Negi told local media.
No suicide note was found and the body was sent for post-mortem examination as investigators look into the circumstances.
Koli first drew national attention in 2006, when he was a domestic worker at businessman Moninder Singh Pandher's home in Noida. The discovery of human remains, including children's, in a drain behind Pandher's house sparked a major investigation and nationwide outrage.
Koli was convicted and sentenced to death in multiple cases beginning in 2009. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both Koli and Pandher for lack of evidence.
Two key observations were made: Koli's confession was inadmissible, as it was extracted after a long, unauthorized interrogation in police custody without adequate legal safeguards, and the prosecution could not prove that the remains uncovered from the "open, public" drain were based solely on Koli's statements.
The decision was upheld by India's Supreme Court in late 2025.
Reports suggest he moved to the northern city of Haridwar after the acquittal. Police identified Koli through an Aadhaar card found on his body.
India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up
A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan.
Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer.
Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India.
"I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony.
The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue."
The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4.
Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team.
A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway.
Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody
The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody.
The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail.
Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding.
He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017.
He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued.
Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary.
"Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture."
Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed.
What did the court say in its ruling?
In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon."
The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached.
Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported.
"I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison."
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from and about India this weekend.
We lead our coverage with the news that British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without conviction, has been granted bail.
A UN panel in 2022 recognized it as a case of arbitrary detention, putting the Indian government's human rights record under the microscope.
The Asian Games kick off in Japan on Saturday, but it's not all smooth sailing for the Indian delegation's preparations.
India has announced a last-minute change of its male flagbearer for the opening ceremony after star shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor's ceremonial kit reportedly went missing.
Finally, counting is underway in elections for the Delhi University Student Union, this time under the shadow of the Cockroach Janata Party protests and the collapse of a building in the student hub of Satya Niketan.
For the latest on these stories and more, follow our blog.

title: For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
content:
For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
When Ziqiang Yuan moved to the U.S. in 1999, democracy was the last thing on her mind. Political speech was suppressed under socialist rule in her native China, and her aversion to politics stayed with her when she emigrated.
“We have a saying in China, ‘不谈政治.’ That means, ‘don't talk about politics,’ ” Yuan said. “You can get in trouble.”
Yuan, 55, goes by Susan now. She left Wuhan for the U.S. to pursue a post-doc in biomedical research, a field that then offered few opportunities in China while demand here was high. She even landed a scholarship.
But when her landlady brought Yuan to a local municipal meeting, eager to show the young grad student what American democracy looked like, something changed in Yuan. She was impressed that ordinary people were even aware of government gatherings, let alone that they could attend.
“That city council meeting really opened my eyes,” Yuan said. “You can have a chance to speak — directly speak — to those officials.”
Decades later, that first brush with local government would lead Yuan to try her chances at politics, a pathway she couldn’t have imagined had she stayed in China.
Yuan is among 175,000 people of Chinese descent who call Massachusetts home, including one in six Quincy residents. For most of U.S. history, Chinese immigrants have journeyed here in hopes of a better life. Their aspirations have varied decade to decade, and person to person. Indeed, ask people in Quincy about the American dream and the answers are as varied as the food options along Hancock and Beale streets.
Interviews with Chinese immigrants spanning multiple generations suggest the allure of the U.S. is being put to the test, amid a torrent of immigration restrictions under President Trump and the emergence of China as the world’s second-largest economy. But for many, the core draw of America remains strong, whether that’s for greater wealth, liberty or cultural freedoms that are elusive in China.
The ’80s generation
On a recent weekend in a downtown event space in Quincy, seniors in classical Chinese attire acted out the myth of the immortal moon goddess.
The Mid-Autumn Festival celebration was organized by Frank Poon of the nonprofit Civic Education Alliance. Poon came to the U.S. during a wave of Chinese immigration in the 1980s. Ronald Reagan was president, Beijing relaxed restrictions on its citizens’ ability to leave the country and the British would agree to transfer Hong Kong to Chinese control.
Poon said he knows success in the U.S. is far from guaranteed — and it often takes a lifetime of struggle.
“We’re still aiming at the American dream,” Poon said, and that people like him are “willing to invest all our time, all our effort, to make it come true.”
Looking back, Poon said he’s achieved what brought him to America 43 years ago. For him, that success has been more spiritual than something that can be measured.
“My American dream is, ‘I want to have a better life,’ ” he said. “I do have a better family. I do have opportunity to work with the community, and deep inside, in my heart and soul, I feel good.”
But one attendee of the harvest festival had something to say about a dream deferred.
In 1988, Carol Chu followed her future husband to Boston, with little money and no family here.
“The United States is such a freedom country,” she said. “I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely.”
Soon after they settled, however, Chu began to realize those things might be out of reach. She became pregnant, and her husband developed a severe gambling addiction. The worst part was when Chu lost custody of her son.
“I [was] so disappointed when I came here, because my American dream totally has not come true,” she said.
Instead of returning to her country, Chu stayed in the U.S. in order to be with her son, even if she could only see him one hour at a time.
"The United States is such a freedom country. I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely."
Carol Chu
Chu recently retired after 37 years working for the Postal Service, and as the years have brought her closer to her son, she said she is finally happy here. Now that her boy is grown, Chu plans to split her time between China and the U.S.
“I think my duty is done,” she said.
Over the decades since these folks emigrated to the U.S., China has roared forward as an economic titan, with hundreds of millions emerging from extreme poverty. For the Chinese youth of today, that adds a new dimension to the decision to leave, whether for the U.S. or anywhere else in the world.
The next generation
At Quincy’s Wollaston Beach, dozens of Chinese youth spread out on the sand, playing mahjong and practicing the Cantonese language. It was a meetup of the Boston Cantonese Club, and DJ Amanda Lou was spinning pop music under a tent.
The recent Boston University graduate is from Macau, a special administrative region of China ruled by the Portuguese until 1999. She spoke about the American ideal more in terms of culture than economic opportunities or political freedom. For her and many other Chinese graduates, Lou said, the exposure to freedom and different lifestyles is a strong motivation to stay.
“In Boston, I can just wear whatever I want, right? I can wear a tank top, shorts, walk outside — nothing will change," she said. "No one's going to stare at you."
At 23, Lou is ready to make a life in Boston. But remaining in the U.S. has never been a certainty for international students. It depends on factors like finding an employer to sponsor a visa petition. And with the current administration looking to add massive fees for foreign worker visas — and to favor “higher-skilled and higher-paid” applicants — big challenges loom for people like Lou.
“What happens if I don't find an employer who's willing to sponsor me?” she said. “Even if they do, what happens if I get fired or something? Definitely very stressful.”
Lou hopes to open a jazz bar in Boston one day, but if America is out of reach, she’ll have to bring her dreams elsewhere.
This kind of uncertainty is well-known to Vincent Lau, an immigration attorney in Boston. Much of his work involves helping American companies secure work visas. Lau said the traditional legal routes still exist, but they have increasingly narrowed under President Trump.
Among an array of measures to tighten rules on student immigration, Lau said consular officers now hold greater discretion to deny visa petitions, making it more difficult to advise parents on the wisdom of sending their kids to the U.S.
“Applying for the visas at the consulates has become much more challenging for Chinese citizens in general,” Lau said, “especially for students.”
On top of that, the administration is cutting research funding and suing elite universities, which Lau said have long been reliable paths to success in America. The administration has threatened to revoke visas for some Chinese students, and it accused Harvard of collaborating with the Chinese Communist Party.
Lau said the draw to study and live in the U.S. remains strong, but those policies are taking a toll.
“When [universities] are not being backed by the government, when they are being attacked by the government, it's not a quote-unquote, safe place,” Lau said. “It's not a place where people want to go.”
The impetus to immigrate has also changed as Chinese universities rise in global rankings. More Chinese youth are pursuing their studies in China. At the same time, an increasing number of students are returning home after graduating overseas.
But for Boston Cantonese Club organizer Alex Ng, China is no promised land. Ng said the Chinese tech economy suffers from a "race to the bottom" mentality, more driven by the search for rock bottom prices than by innovation. Ng said competition for jobs is fiercer in China than in the U.S., and that's especially hard for college grads.
“There are a lot of scientific and technology breakthroughs in China. I'm not discounting that,” said Ng, who holds a master’s in electrical engineering from MIT. “But on the other side, a lot of people graduate from college, they just cannot get a job.”
Born in Hong Kong, Ng moved to Boston from Toronto four years ago. He considers himself lucky that he got his work visa when Joe Biden was president; he worries his peers will now have a harder time.
Ng has yet to achieve his goals of getting married and starting a business. But among his options — and for all this country’s imperfections — Ng said the United States is the place to be. The prestige of the American dream persists, even for a Chinese immigrant who grew up just north of the border.
“First of all, we don't have any Canadian dream,” Ng said with a laugh. “But in Canada, we always heard of the term American dream.”
While many immigrants, like Ng, feel that dream is still a thing, others caution that in one principle area, America could be slipping.
'Liberty is precious'
Sitting outside a Quincy church where two U.S. presidents are interred, Susan Yuan reflected on her path to politics.
After eight years doing research at the University of Vermont and Dartmouth College, she decided to leave academia. She moved to Quincy, and eventually took a job at the Quincy public library.
Soon news out of City Hall started to get under her skin. The council approved a 79% pay hike for the mayor in 2024, and Yuan helped organize a ballot petition to reverse the raise. She was a city employee at the time, and people asked her if she feared retaliation.
“This is America. People should have a right to speak and to petition,” Yuan said. “That's what I learned when I came to U.S.”
"Honestly, I never planned to become a public official. And I don't think that could happen if I'm still in China. So, by that sense, it is a kind of American dream, even though I never dreamed about it."
Yuan’s experience with grassroots activism led her to run for Quincy councilor-at-large. She considered herself a longshot. But she became part of an anti-incumbent wave in the city, and in January, she was sworn in alongside five other new councilors promising to bring change to the city.
“Honestly, I never planned to become a public official,” she said. “And I don't think that could happen if I'm still in China. So, by that sense, it is a kind of American dream, even though I never dreamed about it.”
But Yuan said she worries the U.S. is showing signs of the authoritarianism she left behind.
At the Sept. 8 meeting of the Quincy City Council, dozens of residents showed up to protest the police department's use of Flock Safety’s automated license plate reader cameras. The technology has received pushback from around the country following allegations of misuse by officers, as well as fears the data could be used for immigration enforcement.
Yuan was the first councilor at the meeting to express concern over what she described as a lack of transparency by the city.
“As an immigrant who came from a country in a centralized government, I want to tell you, liberty is precious,” she told the council. “As John Adams said, ‘Liberty once lost is lost forever.’ "
Yuan’s proposal — to hold a hearing on the city’s use of Flock cameras — passed unanimously.
In an interview, Yuan said she experienced mass surveillance during recent visits to China, with cameras watching from all angles. Yuan said surveillance has become so ubiquitous there that some people don’t bother to complain, perhaps because they feel powerless to make change.
“When we see U.S. start to head into that direction, we are more vigilant,” she said.
Now, she wants to help make sure the same doesn’t happen in America. The fact that people are pushing back on surveillance, on the left and the right, she said is a good sign.
This segment aired on September 23, 2026.

title: El camino al subcampeonato: así jugó la Vinotinto sub-20 femenina de futsal
content:
Venezuela se colgó su primera medalla de plata en la historia del torneo Conmebol sub-20 Futsal Femenino. Las catorce jugadoras que conformaron la selección, dirigida por Mike Guerra, plasmaron la mejor participación de la selección durante el torneo que se jugó en el Domo Bolivariano de Barquisimeto. Entre el 12 y 20 de septiembre, jugaron seis partidos y ganaron cuatro de ellos.
La victoria por 2-1 en el debut contra Bolivia representó el inicio goleador de Karlis Durán. Al recibir un pase de la portera Yenixe Flore abrió la cuenta contra las bolivianas, quienes empataron después. La guardameta venezolana fue clave con sus achiques, blocajes y despejes en el arco para mantener a la Vinotinto femenina en el partido. Un córner, ejecutado por María Silveira y que disparó Jhoanyerlis Mejías, derivó en Durán, quien hizo su doblete y concretó la victoria de la selección sub-20.
El primer arco invicto para Flores llegó en la segunda fecha contra Ecuador. La Vinotinto femenina ganó por 0-2 y, aunque no fue tan exigida como ante Bolivia, apareció en el primer palo para despejar un remate. Zharit Fuentes abrió la cuenta para la sub-20, evadiendo a una adversaria al pisar el balón y disparando desde la banda. Para el segundo tanto, Hilmary Chirinos recuperó el balón en la zona medular y asistió a Silveira, quien se desmarcó hacia la derecha, definió de puntera e hizo el segundo gol.
Quedar en la historia
La primera clasificación de la categoría sub-20 de la Vinotinto femenina a unas semifinales de un torneo de futsal ocurrió en la tercera jornada. Una goleada ante Paraguay por el marcador de 1-9 garantizó el pase a la siguiente fase. María Pino, quien no había anotado, hizo cuatro goles. Chirinos marcó un doblete, al igual que Keiberly Salas. Por su parte, Durán sumó el tercero de su cuenta personal.
En el cierre de la fase de grupos, la Vinotinto femenina sub-20 sufrió su primera derrota. Brasil le ganó por 0-3. Con paredes, ataques por las bandas, recuperaciones en la mitad del campo venezolano y un remate de media distancia, las brasileñas golearon a la selección nacional. Pese a la derrota, el boleto a la siguiente etapa estaba asegurado y Venezuela quedó en el segundo lugar de su grupo con nueve puntos.
La fase final
El primer partido de la selección sub-20 de la Vinotinto femenina en la fase decisiva de un torneo de futsal concluyó en una victoria contra Argentina. Las venezolanas se convirtieron en finalistas luego de darle vuelta a un partido en el que estuvieron 2-0 abajo. Pino descontó y anotó su quinto gol del campeonato. Venezuela presionó, recuperó en la mitad del campo argentino y María Rojas puso el 2-2 al definir. El tercer gol, que significó la victoria, surgió de un contraataque finalizado por Michell Fernández.
La Vinotinto femenina sub-20 se volvió a encontrar con Brasil en la final. Una pérdida de Durán terminó en el primer gol de las brasileñas. No obstante, al aprovechar la pelota parada, Silveira remató con su zurda y empató el juego. En un par de ataques a campo abierto, Venezuela perdió el partido y su rival anotó los dos goles para hacer el 1-3 que le dio el título. Pino quedó como máxima goleadora de la selección.

title: Minnesota's 165-mile Mesabi Trail is finally complete after 30 years, among America's longest
content:
Minnesota's Mesabi Trail has reached the finish line after more than three decades of planning, construction, and fundraising, opening a fully paved 165-mile corridor for cyclists, walkers, and skaters across the Iron Range's forests, mining landscapes, and towns.
With the final segment in place, the route stands as one of the longest paved biking trails in the United States and marks the completion of a long-envisioned regional recreation project.
Here's what to know
According to the Good News Network, the Mesabi Trail runs between Grand Rapids and Ely, tying together 28 communities in northeastern Minnesota. Its path carries travelers from the Mississippi River area toward the Boundary Waters through scenery defined by both the natural setting and the Iron Range's mining past.
Users encounter a mix of terrain along the route, with both gentle stretches and steeper sections. Some of the trail's hills trace back to older mining activity, when piles of earth became artificial peaks that later filled back in with forest along the corridor.
The route also offers access to sites connected to the area's past, including historic buildings, mining relics, and places reflecting the Iron Range's ethnic and industrial heritage. That broader history includes the region's role in providing iron ore for the U.S. steel industry and during World War II.
Speaking at the ribbon-cutting ceremony, Iron Range Resources & Rehabilitation Board commissioner Ida Rukavina highlighted how many people and organizations were needed to finish the work: "No single organization, funding source, or individual could have built what we see here today."
More background
Trails like this can also make it easier for people to get around without needing a car for every outing.
Along the Mesabi Trail, access points connect people to campgrounds, parks, and nearby services, making the route practical for a variety of outings. That accessibility can appeal to experienced cyclists as well as families, walkers, and visitors exploring the area.
The route is also meant to stay active outside the height of biking season. Summer use includes hiking and inline skating, while winter brings opportunities for cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, and, in some sections, snowmobile access.
Use already reaches tens of thousands annually.
What's being done?
One of the main contributors was the Department of Iron Range Resources & Rehabilitation, a state agency that reinvests mining profits in local communities, according to GNN.
That approach provided important support for the trail, but completing it still required sustained cooperation from a wide range of partners over many years.
People can use the trail's official website to map out a visit. Supporters can also sign up as volunteer caretakers.
In Rukavina's words, "This trail is the product of three decades of partnership and persistence."
Where can I learn more?
For more on e-bike trail access, rail-based park programs, and long-distance cycling, check out these stories.

• Amtrak and the National Park Service have revived the Trails and Rails program on routes nationwide.

title: Agabeisi es campeón de la Copa Independencia 2026
content:
Agabeisi es campeón de la Copa Independencia 2026
Las "Ardillas" se impusieron 13 carreras por 8 al equipo Bengoa-Zacamil en la Gran Final del Torneo Internacional U10 de béisbol
La novena de la Academia Agabeisi se coronó este domingo campeón del torneo internaciona categoría U10 Copa Independencia 2026, tras derrotar en la gran final al equipo fusionado Bengoa-Zacamil, encuentro que inició en el Parque Saturnino Bengoa, pero que debido a la lluvia fue finalizado en el diamante del Complejo Bengoa.
El Colegio Dominico (Santa Ana) se llevó el tercer lugar al derrotar 13 por 2 a la Academia Hornets de Guatemala.
El torneo organizado por la Federación Salvadoreña de Béisbol, con el apoyo del Instituto Nacional de los Deportes de El Salvador (INDES) contó con tres tres días cargados de buen béisbol, mucha hermandad y compañerismo, así como con varias atracciones para los padres de familia y asistentes al Parque Nacional y su anexo, el denominado Bengoita.
Las ardillas de Agabeisi, dirigidas por Wilfredo Jiménez, remontaron un marcador adverso gracias a una sólida ofensiva encabezada por el primer bate Ian Louico, quien sumó varios extrabases en el torneo, así como un pitcheo combinado muy sólido.
AFJA, la organización nacida en Los Ángeles que usa el deporte para abrir oportunidades
Dylan Romero puso el candado desde la lomita para consolidar la victoria en el choque decisivo.
En el Saturnino Bengoa, Bengoa-Zacamil estaba arriba 4 carreras por 3 mientras cerraba la segunda entrada, pero la lluvia complicó mucho el terreno de juego, por lo que se mudó el choque al Complejo Bengoa, donde Agabeisi dio la vuelta y se llevó el campeonato.
En el duelo por el tercer lugar, el equipo de Santa Ana, Colegio Dominico, se llevó la victoria 13 carreras por 2, ante la novena visitante de Hornets de Guatemala. Los santanecos finalizaron el torneo con paridad de dos triunfos por dos derrotas.
En la primera jornada, el pasado viernes 18 de septiembre, Bengoa-Zacamil derrotó 6 por 5 a Dominico y la Academia Hornets se impuso 14 por 11 a Agabeisi.
El sábado, tras los actos protocolares y una atracción de música en vivo, Agabeisi derrotó 13 por 11 al Dominico y 10 por 4 a Bengoa-Zacamil para clasificar a la final. Bengoa-Zacamil superó a Hornets 13 por 3 y Dominicos hizo lo propio ante los chapines 9 por 3.
Durante el calendario de juego también se realizaron dos juegos de exhibición entre la Selección Nacional U13, que se fogueó con un combinado U14, integrado por jugadores de todas las academias. Los chicos más grandes se llevaron las dos victorias.

title: Freakishly small homes built to match what 25-year-olds can actually afford. Most are smaller than a standard closet
content:
Swedish housing developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics have just built the country’s smallest houses.
They’re not meant to be trendy tiny homes or cute sheds for the backyard; they were built to draw attention to the cost of living crisis among young people.
The three new homes are designed and built to match the average incomes and savings of Sweden’s 25-year-olds. They represent the average statistics across three major cities: Stockholm, Gothenburg, and Umeå.
While that may sound like an ideal setup, to fit within the budgets of Swedish twenty-somethings, the homes are oppressively small, ranging in size from 20 to 48 square feet (or 1.9 to 4.5 square meters).
For reference, the average size of a walk-in closet is 45 to 90 square feet.
Each home appears confiningly cozy, with four simple walls and a roof, a toilet, and a bed that is too small for most adults to actually lay flat in.
Fortunately, the homes are not made to be moved into, but rather, are part of a housing reform campaign to show the affordability crisis at scale.
“Stockholm, Gothenburg, and Umeå are among the Swedish cities where young people have a particularly strong need for housing, while also facing significant difficulties finding and affording it,” BBDO Nordics art director Anton Bolin told Dezeen.
“Together, the three cities show that the issue affects young people across Sweden, from south to north.”
The sizes of the three homes were based on Riksbyggen’s Square Meter Index, which combines income, property prices, and mortgage conditions to show what is affordable to young people who make average incomes in various Swedish cities.
In Umeå, the average young person could afford a 48-square-foot home (the biggest of the three cities). In Gothenburg, the average affordable house comes in at 33 square feet, and in Stockholm, an affordable home would account for just 20 square feet.
“The idea is to make the housing crisis facing young people visible and tangible,” Bolin said.
“We see numbers and statistics about it everywhere, but they can easily become abstract. So we wanted to show exactly how much home an average 25-year-old can afford today, and let people experience that reality.”
On Riksbyggen’s website, each of the three models is described with tongue-in-cheek seriousness, similarly to how realtors depict luxurious properties for sale.
The tiny Stockholm model is called a “turn-of-the-century dream with consistent limitations.”
“Here you live in an environment where the historic architecture creates a dreamlike atmosphere, while the surface sets the framework for a realistic existence,” the description reads.
“In its 1.9 exclusive square meters, the bedroom, living room, kitchen, and bathroom coexist in an unusually cohesive symbiosis. Storage is included in the living space.”
The homes are designed to be inviting, as if they came right out of an Ikea catalogue. But they have been shrunken down to an absurd scale, matching the shocking nature of housing costs.
In addition to making a real statement about the inaccessibility of home ownership for young people, Riksbyggen has a call to action: Introduce three housing reforms.
Those reforms include boosting housing production, making lower-cost loans available to first-time buyers, and reintroducing a program that builds social housing for the elderly, which would make more homes available to younger buyers.
And so far, the designs have stirred interest. Sweden’s housing minister, Andreas Carlsson, has visited the homes — and even attempted to lie on a tiny bed inside, with little success.
“We see real political momentum behind all three proposals, although to varying degrees,” Riksbyggen’s CEO, Johanna Frelin, told Fast Company. “The strongest political support currently seems to be for a state-backed start loan for first-time buyers, while investment support for housing for older people is also gaining renewed attention.
“Our proposal for the state to share more of the risk in new housing construction is more politically challenging,” Frelin continued, “but the need for action is increasingly recognized. Ultimately, we hope the campaign can help turn that recognition into concrete policy.”

title: Polka 20 lat pracowała w Niemczech, teraz wyliczyli jej emeryturę. „Myślałam, że to błąd”
content:
Kobieta, której historię opisał Onet, wyjechała do pracy w Niemczech w 2005 r. po śmierci męża. Miała wówczas 41 lat. W Polsce pod opieką matki zostawiła nastoletnie dzieci. Zrezygnowała też ze swojej pracy w piekarni.
W Niemczech zatrudniła się jako opiekunka osób starszych. Wszystko po to, aby zapewnić swojej rodzinie godne życie. Początkowo planowała wyjazd na kilka miesięcy. Ostatecznie u naszych zachodnich sąsiadów pracowała przez 20 lat. W tym czasie regularnie odprowadzała składki.

20 lat pracy w Niemczech. Tyle wyniesie emerytura Polki
Pani Elżbieta w 2025 r. w wieku 61 lat, po przepracowaniu 20 lat w Niemczech, zwróciła się z prośbą do Deutsche Rentenversicherung (DRV) – tamtejszego odpowiednika ZUS – o wyliczenie przyszłej emerytury. Jak przyznała, nie liczyła na szczególnie wysokie świadczenie. Miała jednak nadzieję, że emerytura będzie w stanie zapewnić jej stabilne życie i poczucie bezpieczeństwa.
Jednak po otrzymaniu wyliczenia przyznała, że była „mocno zaskoczona”. Okazało się bowiem, że jej przyszła emerytura ma wynieść od 520 do 600 euro miesięcznie, czyli obecnie ok. 2200 – 2600 zł.
Czytaj więcej
Pojawia się coraz więcej stron internetowych, które podszywają się pod polskie marki. W swoich ofertach podkreślają korzystne ceny i wysoką jakość....
- Myślałam, że to błąd. Ludzie mówili, że w Niemczech emeryci żyją jak w reklamach. Ale żeby otrzymać te „niemieckie luksusy”, trzeba pracować dwa razy dłużej niż ja – przyznała kobieta w rozmowie z serwisem.
Okazuje się, że wysokość jej przyszłej emerytury to standardowa kwota dla osób, które przez 20 lat pracy w Niemczech zarabiały na poziomie przeciętnej lub nieco poniżej. Przy pełnym stażu pracy średnia niemiecka emerytura wynosi ok. 1800 euro.
Emerytury w Niemczech. Liczba Polaków pobierających niemieckie emerytury rośnie
Na wysokość emerytury w Niemczech wpływa kilka czynników. Najważniejsze z nich to długość okresu składkowego oraz wysokość zarobków. Pełne świadczenie można otrzymać po 45 latach pracy.
O wysokości emerytury decyduje system punktowy, w którym liczba punktów zależy od relacji wynagrodzenia do średniej krajowej. Aby wyliczyć wysokość emerytury, zgromadzone punkty mnoży się przez odpowiednie współczynniki.

Średnia emerytura wypłacana Polakom w Niemczech w 2024 r. wynosiła ok. 823 euro (w przeliczeniu obecnie ok. 3570 zł), wynika z danych DRV przekazanych serwisowi WP Finanse. W tym samym czasie, jak wynika ze statystyk ZUS, średnia emerytura w Polsce wynosiła ok. 3500 zł brutto.
Okazuje się, że liczba Polaków pobierających emerytury w Niemczech regularnie rośnie.
- W 2015 r. wypłacono łącznie prawie 46 tys. emerytur obywatelom polskim. W 2020 r. – prawie 90 tys. W 2024 r. liczba ta wzrosła do ponad 111 tys. – podała serwisowi WP Finanse Katja Braubach z DRV.

title: Introducing Nurse Navigators to Improve Pain Management in the Community.
content: Chronic pain among adults is a highly prevalent condition characterized by persistent gaps in care delivery, inequitable access to evidence-based interventions, and variable care continuity across clinical settings. Nurse Navigators are strategically positioned to help eliminate barriers by assisting in care coordination and person-centered resource maximization. A community-based nurse-led telehealth pilot program was implemented in the Northwestern United States as an extension of a state-funded evidence-based, online platform designed to promote nonpharmacologic pain management options and opioid risk reduction. This initiative offered structured one-to-one virtual consultations and facilitated use of digital self-assessment and educational resources. A convenience sample of adults (≥18 years) with self-reported chronic pain of at least 3 months' duration was recruited via email listservs. Eligible participants completed an initial videoconference session with a Pain Nurse Navigator and a follow-up session 10-14 days later. Ten adults (80% female; mean age 65) with chronic pain participated and completed the follow-up survey. Most either agreed or strongly agreed that they felt comfortable in the sessions with the Pain Nurse Navigator (100%) and were satisfied with the ease of participation (100%) and level of support (90%) provided by the Pain Nurse Navigator. The median Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8 score was 26, indicating acceptable levels of satisfaction for the program. This pilot project established that a nurse-led pain navigation program can be delivered to adults living in a community setting, is acceptable to participants, and generated sufficient satisfaction scores to warrant further study. The model may be adaptable in other settings pending outcome evaluation.

title: 3.25 million digital identities activated through Sanad app
content:
Ammon News - The number of digital identities activated through the government’s Sanad application has reached 3.25 million, according to the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship, which confirmed that the majority of digital identity users are Jordanians.
The ministry said 87.5% of government services have been digitized.
The ministry had previously said that the number of active Sanad users reached around 320,000 per day during August and September.
Minister of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship Sami Smirat had affirmed that the government is committed to automating all government services that can be digitized, totaling 2,400 services.
Smirat added that all digital government services currently being digitized, undergoing process re-engineering, or being re-digitized will be added to the Sanad application.
Organ Donation
Regarding the number of people registered to donate organs through Sanad, the ministry said the figure has now exceeded 29,000, with those users expressing their willingness to donate their organs through the application.
Director of the Sanad application Mohammad Al-Bataikhi said in a previous interview that adding the organ donation service to the application had led to a significant increase in registrations. He explained that users can register by updating the application and accessing the donation icon on the homepage.
Al-Bataikhi added that, after accessing the service, users can review the religious ruling concerning organ donation and then confirm their phone number. Their intention to donate will subsequently appear in the digital family record for all family members.
He explained that the service currently allows citizens to register their willingness to donate organs without specifying particular organs, noting that work is underway to add an option allowing individuals to specify which organs they wish to donate in the event of their death in the future.
Al-Bataikhi said the number of registered donors continues to rise amid growing interest in the service.
Jordan’s General Iftaa Department has permitted organ donation after death to save patients’ lives, subject to religious and medical guidelines, affirming that organ donation falls within acts of charity, solidarity and preservation of life.
Health Minister Ibrahim Al-Badour had said that making the organ donation registration service available through Sanad would be followed by the development of a comprehensive national protocol governing organ donation and transplantation, with the participation of the medical, legal and religious sectors.
The protocol aims to regulate organ donation and transplantation procedures, define the roles of relevant authorities, and ensure that the medical, legal and religious aspects of the process are properly addressed.
The government had approved the addition of the organ donation service to the Sanad application in a bid to encourage and facilitate greater participation in the humanitarian initiative, describing it as an expression of the highest values of human and social solidarity.

title: L’Alliance des jeunes pour la paix et le développement offre des fournitures scolaires aux orphelins des FDS et VDP tombés au front
content:
Burkina-Sécurité-Solidarité
L’Alliance des jeunes pour la paix et le développement offre des fournitures scolaires aux orphelins des FDS et VDP tombés au front
Ouagadougou, 17 sept. 2026 (AIB)- L’Alliance des jeunes pour la paix et le développement au Burkina Faso a offert jeudi, des fournitures scolaires aux enfants des Forces de défense et de sécurités et des volontaires pour défense de la patrie, tombés sur le champ d’honneur. En tout 450 cahiers de 100 pages, 150 cahiers de 200 pages, 150 ardoises, 600 stylos à bille ainsi que des gommes, règles, crayons de papier et gourdes ont été distribués.
Les enfants des forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et des Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie pour la patrie (VDP) tombés au front bénéficieront de kits scolaires pour la rentrée 2026-2027.
L’initiative est de l’Alliance des jeunes pour la paix et le développement au Burkina Faso (AJPD-BF) à l’endroit de la Brigade des volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (BVDP).
Des fournitures scolaires composées de 450 cahiers de 100 pages, 150 cahiers de 200 pages, 150 ardoises, 600 stylos à bille, 150 gommes, 150 règles de 20 cm, 100 ardoises, 150 crayons de papier et 45 gourdes.
Une initiative citoyenne qui vise à garantir l’accès à l’école aux pupilles de la nation et soulager financièrement les veuves et tuteurs et traduire la reconnaissance de la nation envers le sacrifice de leurs parents.
Pour Percey Khaled Gnassounou, secrétaire général de l’alliance, ces fournitures constituent un message d’espoir et de reconnaissance envers les enfants de ceux qui ont sacrifié leur pour la patrie.
« Aujourd’hui ce ne sont pas de simples kits scolaires que nous remettons à ces enfants. Nous voulons leur dire qu’ils ne sont pas seuls. Le sacrifice de leurs parents n’est pas oublié » a confié le camarade Gnassounou.
« L’école reste pour ces enfants, un chemin vers la dignité, la réussite et la construction d’un Burkina Faso meilleur » a affirmé Khaled Gnassounou.
L’Alliance des jeunes pour la paix et le développement au Burkina Faso a appelé les associations sœurs à emboiter leurs pas afin de garantir une éducation de qualité aux enfants des FDS et VDP tombés au front.
